plain grep beat semantic search.

Perplexity described how its agents work inside Projects last week. every project is a git repo. each agent gets its own short-lived sandbox and commits to a shared repository on S3, and fewer than 2% of submissions collide. the search layer is the part worth sitting with: the agents find things with plain ls and grep, and on financial document analysis that beat semantic search on answer accuracy, 63% to 37%.

two lessons in one setup. first, structure beats cleverness. a boring repo with a clear file layout let many agents work in parallel with almost no conflicts. second, retrieval an agent can reason about outperforms retrieval it has to trust. grep returns an exact match it can verify. an embedding returns "probably relevant."

the default that costs you: reaching for vector search and an orchestration framework before you have organised the files.

what I do: before any agent touches a codebase or a document set, I write the architecture rules first. folder layout, naming, what lives where, what the agent may change. agents follow structure extremely well and invent it badly.

the check: ask the agent where a given piece of logic lives. if it has to search semantically to answer, the structure isn't carrying its weight.

I use a prompt that sets exactly this up. it puts the model in the lead-architect seat and makes it follow your architecture rules before it writes code.

Perplexity reports fewer than 2% of agent submissions collide under that setup.

the architecture-first prompt, rules before code:

https://godofprompt.ai/prompt-library/build-full-stack-software-architectures
follow if you want agents that follow your structure instead of inventing their own.

The window is closing for people with below average ability.

To date, you could win on any medium with below average attributes. 

The effort moat was high enough to create favorable supply/demand if you just showed up consistently

That window is closing.

The peak human content with actual top 1% ability will of course always cut through.

Most people reading this are not in that category.

There’s a huge benefit in having built an embedded awareness with 25-50K people.

Those that have that now will be able to take advantage of that instant recognition/trust moving forward.

For those that don’t, with below average abilities (half of people by definition), the easy window will have closed and scaling from 0 to 50K will get much harder.

text: @kanekallaway @scaling_to_100k 🔥 this I will tune into

Every added layer of complexity in an application makes it 10x harder to describe and make content on. 

Back in April I was making many videos on Codex. 

"Codex, OpenAI's version of Claude Code" 
"Codex, the desktop app on your computer"
"Codex, the super app that can do any CPU task"

Very, very easy to describe. 
Repeatable, and viral. 

This made it effortless to describe on short form or long from videos.

Then ChatGPT and Codex merged. 

Okay, now Codex is not an app. 
Codex is a feature inside ChatGPT. 

"Codex, the AI coding agent feature inside the ChatGPT Desktop app"

Okay, now ChatGPT has "GPT Work"

"Codex, the AI coding agent feature inside the ChatGPT desktop app that allows you to do coding tasks, and sometimes work tasks, some of those should be done inside GPT Work, which is kind of similar, but like different, depending on if you are using Cloud GPT Work, or local GPT work, in which case is alot closer to Codex, but still not quite the same. If you try and use the skills you created on Codex they won't work when doing a cloud GPT Work session but if it's a local session it will work."

We haven't even made it to Codex Cloud sessions, GPT Dots, and GPT Plugins yet. 

This goes for anyone building software. If you want to create an ecosystem of creators who talk about your product organically, you should aim for simplicity.

BTW not saying it was the wrong decision for OpenAI to merge them, i'm just saying for me it got much harder to describe with every new feature added.
